sectionsContent.title: Ionization Energy & Electronegativity

concept.summary: Ionization energy is the energy needed to pull one electron off an atom. Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on electrons it shares in a bond. Both rise across a period and fall down a group.
keyIdeas: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity, 4.0. Noble gases are usually left off electronegativity tables because they rarely bond.

sectionsContent.directions: Use the trends, not a data table. A periodic table is allowed.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what is electronegativity?
questions.solution: How strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it shares with another atom in a bond. Accept any wording that includes pulling on shared electrons. Do not accept 'energy to remove an electron' (that is ionization energy).
questions.finalAnswer: an atom's pull on shared electrons in a bond

questions.prompt: Which element has the highest electronegativity of all?
questions.solution: Fluorine (4.0), top right of the table, not counting the noble gases.

questions.prompt: Rank these from lowest to highest electronegativity: Na, Cl, P, Mg.
questions.solution:
All four are in period 3, so electronegativity rises left to right: Na < Mg < P < Cl.
Values for reference: Na 0.93, Mg 1.31, P 2.19, Cl 3.16.

questions.prompt: Rank these from lowest to highest ionization energy: Cs, Li, K.
questions.solution:
All three are in group 1, so ionization energy falls going down: Cs < K < Li.
Values for reference (kJ/mol): Cs 376, K 419, Li 520.
Common error: ranking by atomic number in the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: Oxygen's electronegativity is 3.4 and sulfur's is 2.6. Selenium sits directly below sulfur. Predict a value for selenium and give the trend you used.
questions.solution:
Any value below 2.6 (and above about 2.0) with the reason 'electronegativity decreases down a group'.
Actual value: 2.55. Full credit for the trend and a value under 2.6; the exact number is not the point.
questions.finalAnswer: below 2.6 (actual 2.55); EN decreases down a group

questions.prompt: Metals sit on the left of the table and have low ionization energy and low electronegativity. Using what the Gizmo showed you about atomic radius, explain why.
questions.solution:
Atoms on the left of a period are the largest in that period (Gizmo, 3.3). Their outer electrons are far from the nucleus and held loosely, so little energy removes one (low IE) and they pull weakly on shared electrons (low EN).
Grading: 1 point for large radius on the left, 2 points for outer electrons far from the nucleus / weakly held, 1 point for linking that to both IE and EN.
questions.finalAnswer: large atoms, outer electrons far away and loosely held, so low IE and low EN

sectionsContent.title: Explaining Periodic Trends

concept.summary: Two things set every trend. Nuclear charge: more protons pull harder on the electrons. Energy levels: each new level puts the outer electrons farther out, behind more inner electrons that block part of the pull.
keyIdeas: Same period: compare protons. Same group: compare energy levels.

sectionsContent.directions: For every 'explain', name the trend, compare the two atoms, and say what causes the difference.

questions.prompt: Moving left to right across period 3, what happens to the number of protons?
questions.solution: It goes up by one with each element (Na 11 to Ar 18).

questions.prompt: Moving down group 1, what happens to the number of energy levels?
questions.solution: It goes up by one with each period (Li 2, Na 3, K 4 ...).

questions.prompt: Which atom is larger, magnesium or sulfur? Explain using nuclear charge.
questions.solution:
Magnesium. Both are in period 3 with the same three energy levels. Sulfur has 16 protons to magnesium's 12, so it pulls the same levels in tighter.
Values for reference: Mg 160 pm, S 103 pm (textbook values vary by source).
questions.finalAnswer: magnesium; S has more protons pulling on the same levels

questions.prompt: Which has the lower ionization energy, lithium or cesium? Explain using energy levels.
questions.solution:
Cesium. It has six energy levels to lithium's two, so its outer electron is much farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.
Values: Cs 376 kJ/mol, Li 520 kJ/mol.
questions.finalAnswer: cesium; outer electron is farther out

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Chlorine is smaller than sodium because chlorine has more electrons." What is wrong with this reasoning? Give the correct reason.
questions.solution:
More electrons by themselves would not shrink an atom; electrons repel each other. The real cause is the protons: chlorine has 17 to sodium's 11, and both use three energy levels, so chlorine pulls its electrons in closer.
Grading: 1 point for rejecting 'more electrons', 2 points for more protons with the same energy levels.
questions.finalAnswer: electrons do not shrink an atom; more protons on the same levels do

questions.prompt: Potassium's outermost electron is in energy level 4. Sodium's is in energy level 3. Potassium's first ionization energy is 419 kJ/mol and sodium's is 496 kJ/mol. Explain why potassium's is lower, and say which element in group 1 you expect to be lowest of all.
questions.solution:
Potassium's outer electron is one energy level farther out, with more inner electrons blocking the nucleus, so less energy removes it. The trend continues down the group, so the lowest is at the bottom: francium (or cesium, the lowest that is actually measured well; accept either).
Grading: 2 points for farther out / more shielding, 1 point for linking to less energy, 1 point for the bottom of the group.
questions.finalAnswer: farther out and more shielded; francium (accept cesium)

sectionsContent.title: Ion Formation

concept.summary: Metals lose electrons and become cations (positive). Nonmetals gain electrons and become anions (negative). For main-group elements, the group number tells you the charge: group 1 is 1+, group 2 is 2+, group 13 is 3+, group 15 is 3−, group 16 is 2−, group 17 is 1−.
keyIdeas: A cation is smaller than its atom. An anion is larger than its atom.

sectionsContent.directions: Write charges after the symbol, number first: Mg2+, O2−.

questions.prompt: A cation has a positive charge. Did the atom gain or lose electrons?
questions.solution: Lost electrons. Fewer electrons than protons leaves a positive charge.

questions.prompt: Write the ion formed by potassium and the ion formed by bromine.
Write the ion formed by each: aluminum, oxygen, nitrogen, strontium.
questions.solution: Al3+ (group 13), O2− (group 16), N3− (group 15), Sr2+ (group 2). Half a point each.

questions.prompt: Which is larger, Mg or Mg2+? Which is larger, F or F−? Explain one of your answers.
questions.solution:
Mg is larger than Mg2+: losing two electrons empties magnesium's outer energy level.
F− is larger than F: same 9 protons now hold 10 electrons that repel each other, so the ion spreads out.
Values: Mg 160 pm, Mg2+ 72 pm; F 64 pm, F− 133 pm.

questions.prompt: F−, Na+ and Mg2+ each have exactly 10 electrons. Rank them from smallest to largest and explain using protons.
questions.solution:
Mg2+ < Na+ < F−. All three have the same 10 electrons in the same two energy levels. Mg2+ has the most protons (12), then Na+ (11), then F− (9), so Mg2+ pulls hardest and is smallest.
Values: Mg2+ 72 pm, Na+ 102 pm, F− 133 pm.
Common error: ranking by charge sign alone without mentioning protons; give 1 of 3.
questions.finalAnswer: Mg2+ < Na+ < F−; more protons on the same 10 electrons

questions.prompt: Sodium could reach a noble-gas arrangement by losing 1 electron or by gaining 7. Which does it do? Use ionization energy and electronegativity in your answer.
questions.solution:
Sodium loses 1 electron and becomes Na+. Its ionization energy is low (496 kJ/mol), so its single outer electron comes off easily, and its electronegativity is low (0.93), so it pulls weakly on extra electrons; gaining seven is far harder.
Grading: 1 point for Na+, 1.5 points for low IE, 1.5 points for low EN.
questions.finalAnswer: loses 1 to form Na+; low IE and low EN
